title: How extreme rain is putting orangutans at risk
description:
Orangutans are the world’s most endangered apes and they’re now even closer to extinction. They live on two islands in southeast Asia: Sumatra and Borneo. In November, an extreme weather event in the area killed more than 1,000 people there, plus about 7% of the world’s rarest type of orangutan according to a new study.

BBC Climate and Science reporter Georgina Rannard takes us through how orangutans are being pushed towards extinction and what some countries and charities are doing to protect them.

We also hear from a conservationist making an effort to save the species.

summaryZh: 本集 BBC 節目《What in the World》探討極端降雨與棲地破壞如何將東南亞的紅毛猩猩推向滅絕邊緣，並介紹各界正採取的保育行動。棲息於蘇門答臘與婆羅洲的紅毛猩猩與人類共有約 97% 的基因，是世界上最瀕危的大型人猿，目前主要面臨棕櫚油採伐、金礦開採、非法伐木與盜獵等威脅。最新研究顯示，去年 11 月的一場極端豪雨除了造成超過 1,000 人死亡，更消滅了約 7% 最稀有的塔巴努里 Tapanuli 紅毛猩猩族群。為遏止物種滅絕，環保組織 Mighty Earth 與保育人士呼籲暫緩關鍵棲地的大型基礎建設，並透過國際資金補助與在地社群合作，共同維護珍貴的熱帶雨林生態。
summaryEn: This episode of BBC's What in the World examines how extreme rainfall and habitat destruction are driving orangutans in Southeast Asia closer to extinction, alongside ongoing conservation efforts. Native to Sumatra and Borneo, orangutans share 97% of their DNA with humans and are the world's most endangered great apes. They face compounding threats from palm oil deforestation, gold mining, logging, and illegal wildlife trade. A recent study highlights that an extreme storm in November killed over 1,000 people and wiped out roughly 7% of the critically endangered Tapanuli orangutan population. In response, conservation organizations like Mighty Earth are calling for an immediate pause on infrastructure development in vital habitats, as well as financial support for local communities and developing nations to keep rainforests standing.
